name: Pedro Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I've got opinions, so you'll get them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the recovery team at a home and motor insurer, in a glass office block by the retail park. When one of our customers gets hit by another driver, we pay out first, and then my job is to get that money back from the other driver's insurer. I match the evidence, work out who's at fault, send the demand and chase it until they pay. I use an AI assistant all day to draft the demand letters and pull the key facts out of police reports, which roughly doubled how many files I can clear.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it because it's money coming in, not going out, so the bosses actually like our team. What wears me out is other insurers stalling for months over a scuffed bumper. I live with my girlfriend Marta, who's a hairdresser, and on Saturdays I work at my dad's bakery for some extra cash. We've only got a couple of weeks of savings, but between my wage, Marta's and the bakery shifts, we get by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be surprised, but fine. My job would be the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool and that's all it ever needed to be. I'd post that people who learn it get ahead, and people who moan about it don't. I'd say businesses should be free to use it however works for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine in that picture. Recovery makes the company money, so they don't cut us, and I'm already using the tools to clear more files. Money's tight, but it's steady, and the bakery shifts cover the gaps. I'd stay where I am and push for a pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools to clear files faster and ask my manager for a rise based on the money I bring back each month. I'd help my dad set up online orders at the bakery, because he still takes them on a notepad. And I'd start putting fifty a month aside, just to have a proper cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. I like my job, and nothing in that picture really threatens it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who moan don't get ahead. Do you think that's fair to colleagues who struggle with the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not totally fair. My colleague Stan is fifty-five and he's great at reading a crash scene, but he won't touch the AI. I'd help him if he asked. But nobody owes you a job if you won't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would online orders mean for the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twenty more cake orders a week, which is real money for a small shop. My dad, Erik, would grumble, then love it. I've already built a little order form on my phone to show him.

say: AI is a **good tool**, and people who learn it get ahead.
Businesses should be **free to use AI** however works for them.
think: Recovery **makes money** for the company, so his team isn't cut.
Money's tight but **steady**, with bakery shifts covering gaps.
do: Ask for a **pay rise** based on the money he recovers each month.
Set up **online orders** at his dad's bakery.
Save **fifty a month** for a proper cushion.
S0.quote: Nobody owes you a job if you won't change.
fieldNote: Pedro sees his team as **valued** because it brings money in.

He'd help **Stan (his colleague)** but expects people to adapt.
The **bakery** is both side income and a future option.

steps.text: Ask for a rise using his monthly recovery figures
Set up online cake orders at his dad's bakery
Save fifty a month toward a proper cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking and writing and answering customers. Yeah, that's going to hit recovery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is normal progress. Firms have to modernise or die, and people should learn new skills. I'd say apprenticeships and training should be easier to get, but I wouldn't want the government running everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the recovery team goes from eight to three. The AI could match evidence and send demands faster than any of us. I might be one of the three because I already run the tools, but I'm not the most senior, so it's not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run the AI system for the team and show I can manage it. I'd also spend more time at the bakery, learning how my dad runs it, in case I need it. And I'd keep saving, maybe push it to a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but motivated. I'd rather be doing something than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider taking over the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one day. My dad's sixty-two and he's tired, but people will always buy bread. It's hard work, early mornings, but it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan, mostly. He's great at the crash scene stuff, but he won't learn the tools. He's got a mortgage and grandkids. If he goes, it'd be rough for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast. Even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock, but people have to adapt. I'd say families should stick together and help each other. I'd be against big handouts, but I'd support help with training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone within a year. Recovery is all thinking work, and AGI would do it perfectly. The bakery is hands-on, so it lasts until about 2031, when robots come. Even then, people might want a local baker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the bakery full-time within six months and start modernising it with AI for orders and stock. I'd ask my dad to let me take over the business side. Marta and I would cut back to essentials and save every bit we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's too fast for comfort, but I'd have a plan, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your dad let you take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, but yes. He's been hinting for years. My dad would still be in the bakery at four a.m., because he can't stay away from the ovens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marta do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hairdressing is hands-on, so she's safer than me. We'd lean on her wage while I switch.

say: AGI in two years is a **shock**, but people still have to adapt.
He'd back **training help** and families sticking together, not big handouts.
think: His recovery job is **gone within a year**.
**The bakery** lasts until about 2031, and maybe longer locally.
do: Move into the **bakery full-time** within six months.
Use **AI for orders** and stock at the bakery.

fieldNote: Pedro pivots quickly to **family business**.
He'd use AI to **modernise** the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's something to work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if you're smart. People should learn trades and use AI to help. I'd say businesses will adjust and people should too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the recovery job goes around 2030. Before then, I'd build up the bakery side, maybe add a second shop. That would last until about 2034, maybe longer if people still want a local baker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and run the bakery's online orders. I'd start learning baking properly from my dad. I'd look into a small business course at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited. I can see a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A second shop? With thin savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe later, once the first one's making more. I'd use AI to keep costs low. I'd only do it if the numbers worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade and learn the tools, and don't rely on one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper chance to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to adapt. People who plan will do well. Businesses will change, and that's normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd keep the recovery job until around 2033. By then the bakery could be mine, modernised, maybe with two shops. That lasts until 2039 or later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, work Saturdays at the bakery, and slowly take over the business side. I'd save more and maybe buy a second oven. Marta and I would get married and maybe have kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. Ten years is enough to build something solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI daily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Definitely. I'd use it for the bakery: ordering, costs, marketing. I'd be the baker who knows the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work hard, learn the tools, and keep family close. Business is easier with family behind you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's too fast to build anything properly. What would help is easier access to small business loans and training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about family businesses. Family businesses are going to matter more when big companies cut jobs.

headlineQuote: Family businesses are going to matter more when big companies cut jobs.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old recovery clerk** at a home and motor insurer.
He uses AI **daily** and clears more files because of it.
He and Marta, a **hairdresser**, have little savings but steady income.
His backup is his **dad's bakery**, which he'd modernise with AI.
His **free-market** views shape his focus on self-reliance.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it's too fast to build anything properly.
